body: You held the door on the coldest day of the year, and you were not even going my way. I have thought about it more than seems reasonable. My hands were full, my heart was fuller of worse things, and you simply stood there, patient as furniture, until I passed.

I never learned your name. That is the strange arithmetic of kindness: the people who change the weather of a day are so often the ones we cannot thank. So I am thanking the air instead, and anyone standing in it. If a stranger holds a door for you this week, it might be the same weather, moving on.
letters.firstLine: To the stranger who held the door:
letters.title: The Door

body: Sit down a moment. The tea is only warm, but that will do.
Everything you are afraid of losing is already teaching you how much of it was love. That is not a small thing to know. Most people go their whole lives calling it fear.

You will lose some of it. You will also find, in the losing, that your hands were built for holding more than one thing at a time: the grief, and the groceries, and somebody's small warm hand crossing the street.
Write back when you can. I am rooting for you in the tense you are not using yet.
letters.firstLine: Dear future self, on an ordinary morning:
letters.title: Ordinary Morning

body: I stood at the shore in the hour when the light gives up politely, and the water did what it has done longer than anything on land has been alive to watch. It came in. It went out. It did not explain itself, and I found I did not need it to.
People ask what the sea means. I think the sea is what meaning looks like before we get our hands on it.
Come and stand here sometime. Bring nothing to solve. The tide will do its old work on your thoughts, the way it does on stones: kindly, and over time.
letters.firstLine: To the ocean, which was here first:
letters.title: Here First

body: You taught a room of tired fourteen-year-olds that a sentence could be a place to live. I was the quiet one by the window. I am not quiet anymore, and it is partly your doing.
I still have the book you pressed on me, the one you said I was not ready for. You were right about that too; I grew into it the way you knew I would.
Teachers plant things in weather they will never stand in. Consider this a report from your climate: it is raining here, gently, and everything you planted is up.
letters.firstLine: Dear Mrs. A, wherever you are teaching now:
letters.marginNote: In the margin, in a different hand: “She kept the book. They always keep the book. C.”
letters.title: The Book

body: I have started leaving the porch light on for you, which is foolish, because you are made of light half the month anyway. But habit is a kind of prayer, and I am out of the other kind.

You have seen every version of me: the one dancing in a kitchen, the one crying into a sink at 3 a.m., the one who finally, finally slept. You never once looked away. There are friends I cannot say that about.
Next month, same window. I will bring the good blanket. You bring the silver.
letters.firstLine: To the moon, a regular correspondent:
letters.title: Same Window

body: I am writing to the gap in the group photograph, which is to say, to you.

We were a constellation once; nobody told us stars drift. If you are well, let the drift be forgiven. If you are not well, let this reach you like a hand on a shoulder in a crowd: brief, certain, gone before it can embarrass either of us.
The song we liked came on in a shop last week. I stayed until it finished. That is all. That is the whole letter, really.
letters.title: The Photograph

body: You do not know me, and if the system works, you never will. This house will be somebody else's kitchen someday, and my handwriting will be under the third stair, where the board lifts.

Here is what I can tell you from upstream: the light in the back room is best in October. The pipes sing in January; it is not a fault, it is a feature we learned to love. Someone small once grew an inch a year against the pantry door, and we painted over it, and I am sorry about that most of all.
Live loudly in the mornings. The house likes it.
letters.postscript: P.S. You came back. So did I. Some letters are just doors that learned patience.
letters.title: The Stair

body: You are the most underpraised accomplice. Every garden, every apology, every second first impression I have ever made began with you rinsing the slate.

I have met you in hospital corridors and on mountain tops, in the fluorescent hour of airports, holding terrible coffee like a sacrament. You never ask what the night did. You simply begin, again, as if beginning were easy, as if you had not watched me fail at it for years.
It is not easy. I know. Thank you for pretending it is, until it is.
letters.firstLine: To the morning, who keeps forgiving us:
letters.title: Accomplice

body: This is to say I have eaten none of the plums, because they are yours, and because watching you wait for them all summer has become one of my summer's pleasures.
Grow slow things. Grow more than you need. Grow one row for the neighbours you have not met and one for the bees, who are the only honest critics.
When the fence leans, we will lean it back. That is the whole philosophy. Everything else is weather.
letters.firstLine: To the garden, and its keeper:
letters.title: One Row for the Bees

longLetters.title: Under This Roof
longLetters.firstLine: To the hands that raised this roof:
body: I do not know your names. I know your work the way you know weather: from inside it. The beam above the kitchen door is level. The stairs do not complain. Somewhere under the floor, a joist you set true before I was born is still holding its line, and holding me with it, every day, without being asked twice.

You will never read this. That is the condition of your trade, and I have come to think it is the condition of most kindness: it is done for strangers, at full care, in the knowledge that the thanks, if it comes at all, will come too late and to the wrong address. So let this be the wrong address, gratefully wrong.

I have tried to imagine the day you framed the back wall. Someone held the other end of the timber. Someone sang, or nobody did, and the hammering was music enough. One of you cut a board a finger short and cut another without being told. One of you was nineteen and certain the work was beneath him, and an older hand showed him, without a word, what beneath a house actually means: everything stands on it.

Did you know a letter would be written in the room you were raising? Did you leave the wall plumb for a person you would never meet, out of nothing but the habit of doing it right when no inspector was coming? I live inside your answer. It is yes. It has been yes every morning, in the small sounds a well-made house makes instead of the sounds of giving up.

There is a pencil mark on a stud behind the plaster, there always is; houses keep one signature that only demolition will ever read. I have decided not to need to see it. Some signatures are for the building. Mine is different: I keep the roof mended. I sweep the step you poured. When the fence leans, we lean it back: you taught me that without meeting me, the way honest work teaches everyone who lives inside it.

Gratitude is supposed to be a feeling, I am told. This room disagrees. Here it is a practice, and you are among its first teachers: care done completely for people who will never know your names. I am practising. When I make a thing for strangers, I make it level. When I leave a thing behind, I leave it true.

Sleep well, whoever you were, in whatever house is holding you now. This one is holding me. The beam is level, the stairs are quiet, and a stranger you never met is standing in your good work, saying thank you to the air, and meaning the air to carry it to you.

longLetters.title: The Chair
longLetters.firstLine: Dear grief, there is a chair for you:
body: You arrived the way weather arrives: without asking, in the middle of other plans. I spent the first season trying to be rid of you. I was polite about it, the way people are polite to a guest they hope will leave before supper. You stayed through supper. You stayed through winter. So I am writing to say what I should have said at the door: sit down. There is a chair for you. It has always been yours; I was only standing in front of it, pretending the room was smaller than it is.

You are not the opposite of love. I know that now, and knowing it cost me the years it cost, so I will say it plainly for whoever is reading over my shoulder: you are love, continuing. You are what love does when the address it had is gone and it refuses, stubborn, faithful, unreasonable, to stop delivering itself. That is why you are heavy. What is carried for the beloved weighs what the beloved weighed.

In the hard months I measured you. A morning when the chair stood empty for an hour felt like a victory, and then you would be in it again by noon, quiet as furniture, and I would call the whole day lost. I do not measure anymore. Some days you sit the whole day and the day is not lost. Some days you are gone by breakfast and I find, to my surprise, that I look for you: out of love's habit, not sorrow's; the way a house listens for a step it has known for years.

You taught me the household arithmetic nobody teaches: that a heart is not a cup, emptied by pouring. It is a house. It can hold the feast and the empty chair at the same table, the song and the silence after it, and there is still room. This is your whole curriculum, grief: still room, at the same table, for joy to sit down without apologising for arriving.

People ask when you will leave, as if your leaving were the happy ending. I have stopped wanting it. What I want is smaller and larger: that you and joy learn the house together, the way old residents do: taking turns at the window, neither one locking the other out. On the good days you nod at each other across the room. I have seen it. It is enough. It is, if I am honest, more than enough: it is a life.

So stay, in your chair, as long as the love that sent you stays, which is to say, stay. I will keep the chair. I will keep the room large. And on the mornings when the light comes in and finds us both here, I will make tea for the house as it is: one cup for the living, one set down anyway, out of practice, out of gratitude, because a practice is how a feeling proves it means to last.
